abstract: Therapeutic genome editing introduces DNA double-strand breaks into hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), making chromosome integrity an important consideration for edited cell function. We investigated how caspase activity influences cellular responses to genome editing in primary human HSPCs. Caspase inhibition increased the fraction of phospho-histone H3-S10-positive cells and reduced micronucleus formation and DNA damage after editing. Genome editing was associated with reduced detection of BUB1 and H2A-T120p at centromeres, with partial restoration after caspase inhibition. Genetic disruption of BUB1 did not fully reproduce the effects of editing, and caspase inhibition continued to increase the phospho-histone H3-S10-positive fraction in BUB1-deficient cells. p53 suppression reduced micronucleus formation without increasing this fraction, distinguishing its effects from those of caspase inhibition. After xenotransplantation, recipients of HSPCs exposed to caspase inhibition in vitro had increased bone marrow cellularity and total CD34+ cell numbers. These findings identify caspase activity as a determinant of cell cycle and chromosome integrity outcomes after genome editing in human HSPCs.
